content:
Mio looked away too quickly.

“They’re going to decide what I am,” she said.

Touma had almost managed a joke. It died before he could say it.

“Who?”

“People.” She glanced toward the doorway. “They’ll look at me, and then they’ll explain me to each other. I’m not sure I get a vote.”

“We don’t have to make this public.”

“Public isn’t the opposite of normal, Touma.”

“I didn’t say it was.”

“You were approaching it with purpose.”

He rubbed his palms against his knees. “I just meant we could take some of the pressure off.”

“You make it sound like you’re offering to remove my nervous system.”

“That’s not what I’m offering.”

“Good. I’ve only just started worrying about it.”

Nico turned toward the hall.

“I’ll be outside.”

He said it with the strained practicality of someone who had found a task called Being Elsewhere. Touma couldn’t blame him. Nico stepped out of the bedroom, though his shadow stayed near the doorway.

The room became smaller.

The air conditioner had gone quiet. Without it, Touma could hear every shift of fabric, every breath he was trying not to take too carefully.

“Do you want to sit down?”

Mio looked at the chair beside the desk.

“Is that a request or a diagnostic?”

“A chair.”

“Excellent. For a moment I thought you were going to check whether I passed through it. Like a haunted projector.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

She sat.

The chair squeaked under her weight.

Touma felt such immediate relief that he couldn’t hide it. The chair had taken her weight. Nothing had flickered or refused or failed. A cheap piece of furniture in a cheap safehouse had made room for her without requiring an explanation.

“Don’t make that face,” Mio said.

“What face?”

“Like the furniture just approved my application.”

“Sorry.”

He sat on the edge of the futon.

She had made it sound ridiculous, which it was. But her fingers were gripping the sides of the seat.

He knew that look now—or thought he did. Fear looked embarrassingly like embarrassment when it had a face. You could mistake it for irritation, for someone wanting you to stop staring. You could oblige and miss what they were afraid of.

“Can you eat?” he asked.

Mio stared at him.

He wished, immediately, that he had chosen any other question.

“I don’t know,” she said.

“Oh.”

“Very useful. We’re making progress.”

“I was thinking I could get you something.”

Her expression shifted a little.

Touma looked down at his hands. Food. Water. Sleep. Pain. He had been reaching for ordinary things he could offer, and every one of them opened into something neither of them knew.

She was sitting right there, and he didn’t know whether being there hurt.

He wanted to take her hand.

His hand moved before he stopped it.

Mio noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You were about to ask something.”

In the hall, Nico’s shadow shifted.

“I’ll go check downstairs,” he said.

“Nico, wait.”

Nico stopped. Touma looked toward him, then couldn’t think of a single reason to make him stay that wasn’t cowardice.

“No. Sorry. Go ahead.”

Nico nodded without looking into the room. His footsteps moved away.

Touma turned back to Mio.

“I was going to ask if it hurt.”

For a moment, the room did something wrong.

The edge of the desk seemed to slide sideways without moving. Mio’s outline lost its agreement with the chair, then snapped back into place. Touma blinked, but the feeling remained: something had strained too hard to hold a shape he could understand.

Mio’s finger twitched against the seat.

“That,” he said quietly. “Did that hurt?”

“I’m trying.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He swallowed. “No. I don’t.”

She looked down at her hand.

“Maybe we need some ground rules,” he said.

“How reassuringly administrative.”

“No surprise touching.”

Her eyes lifted to his.

“From me,” he added. “I won’t touch you without asking.”

“All right.”

“And tell me if something hurts.”

Mio’s mouth tightened.

“I don’t want to be a problem.”

“People are problems.”

“Your bedside manner is extraordinary.”

“I mean people need things. They hurt, and other people have to change what they’re doing. That doesn’t mean they shouldn’t be there.”

She watched him closely enough to make him want to improve what he had said. He resisted.

“If something’s wrong, tell me,” Touma said. “I’ll listen.”

“Even if you can’t see it?”

“Yes.”

“Even if everything looks fine to you?”

“Yes.”

Mio loosened her grip on the chair.

It wasn’t trust. He didn’t think he had earned that yet. But she seemed to be considering whether she might want to believe him.

Then someone appeared in the doorway.

The support technician had one hand braced against the frame, already leaning in to say something. He stopped when he saw Mio.

“Oh,” he said. “Who’s that?”

Mio went perfectly still.

Touma stood too fast. His knee caught the desk, and the noise made the technician flinch.

“Not your business.”

The words were too sharp, too immediate. He heard how they sounded only after they were out.

The technician looked from him to Mio, then back again.

Touma saw the change.

First there had been surprise. Then curiosity. Now there was a story taking shape behind the man’s eyes—a story with a bedroom, a girl, and Touma behaving as though he had something to hide.

It was the wrong kind of miracle. Someone could look at Mio and see a person, and still turn her into something she had never agreed to be.

“Leave,” Touma said.

“I was just—”

“Please.”

The technician lifted his hands and backed into the hall.

Touma shut the door.

For a moment he stayed facing it. His face was hot. So was the back of his neck. Embarrassment and fear had arrived together, and he hated that he couldn’t separate them.

Behind him, Mio said, “Well. There’s my dramatic reveal.”

He turned.

She was still sitting with her hands carefully placed on the chair.

“Mio—”

“That was public.”

“I know.”

“No. Not hypothetical public. Someone saw me.”

“I know.”

It was too late to keep this from becoming a rumor. There had already been one pair of eyes too many. Even if the technician said nothing, he would remember. He had seen her here, and Touma’s reaction had supplied the punctuation.

“What do we do if people start asking?” she said.

“We lie.”

Mio looked at him with something between disgust and reluctant affection.

“That was distressingly quick.”

“I can take longer.”

“Please don’t. You’ll make it worse.”

He almost smiled. She didn’t.

“If I’m going to be seen,” Mio said, “I refuse to be seen as a mistake.”

Touma’s answer came before he could soften it.

“You’re not a mistake.”

The room went quiet again.

There was something dangerous about saying it without a joke attached. He had nothing to hide behind, and neither did she. He could only stand there and mean it.

Mio let out a small, shaky laugh.

It didn’t make her look less afraid.

But for one second, the room was bearable.

Then something scraped outside it.

Touma turned toward the door.

Not footsteps. Not the handle.

The sound came from beside the frame: a soft, slow drag, like a fingertip being drawn along the other side of the wall.

He stared at the plaster.

Nothing moved. Still, he had the sick impression of pressure gathering there, something resting against the wall and gradually putting more of its weight forward.

His limiter pulsed cold.

Not the familiar restraint. Colder than that.

A warning.

Mio rose from the chair.

Touma didn’t look away from the wall. The sound had stopped, but the silence no longer felt empty. Whatever was beyond it seemed to be listening—not merely for where she was, but for an answer it could assign to her.

“Don’t let the system decide what I am,” Mio said.

The wall answered with a deeper scrape, as though it had heard her and leaned closer.
